topics.name: Prescription Principles and Dosage Calculations
topics.description: Essential metric conversions, solution concentration calculations, and prescription documentation rules.

subtopics.name: Metric Conversions and Solutions
subtopics.description: Mathematical relationships between milligrams, grams, micrograms, and percentage solutions.

questions.question: Based on the standard pharmacological dosage conversions provided in the lesson, how many grams are equal to 100 mg?
questions.explanation: According to the conversion guidelines in the lesson, 100 mg equals 0.1 g.

questions.question: A liquid medication has a concentration of 10 mg/ml. What is the corresponding percentage solution?

options.text: 0.1% solution
10% solution
1% solution
0.01% solution

questions.explanation: The conversion reference explicitly indicates that 10 mg/ml corresponds to a 1% solution.

questions.question: According to the conversion reference table in the lesson, what is the value of 1 microgram (1 μg) expressed in grams?
questions.explanation: The lesson conversion table explicitly states that 1 μg is equivalent to 0.0001 g.

subtopics.name: Prescription Blank Specifications
subtopics.description: Rules governing prescription blank notation, validity duration, and special card requirements.

questions.question: Which of the following medications is specifically designated in the lesson with the notation 'Write on yellow card'?

options.text: Diazepam
Amoxicillin / Clavulanic acid
Metoprolol
Omeprazole

questions.explanation: In the lesson prescription notes, Diazepam is specifically annotated with 'Write on yellow card'.

questions.question: On the medical documentation prescription form shown in the lesson, what is the validity duration when 30 days is crossed out?

options.text: 10 days
6 months
1 year
2 months

questions.explanation: The prescription blank at the bottom specifies: 'This prescription is valid for: 30 days 2 months (cross out invalid)'.

topics.name: Antimicrobial and Antiparasitic Pharmacology
topics.description: Mechanisms of action, clinical indications, adverse effects, and drug interactions of antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, and anthelmintic agents.

subtopics.name: Antibacterial Drugs
subtopics.description: Bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics including beta-lactams, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, and lincosamides.

questions.question: What is the primary pharmacological role of clavulanate in the combination drug Amoxicillin / Clavulanic acid?

options.text: Clavulanate enhances amoxicillin absorption across the gastrointestinal mucosa
Clavulanate directly inhibits bacterial protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit
Clavulanate inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase to protect amoxicillin from enzymatic degradation
Clavulanate blocks bacterial dihydrofolate reductase to arrest folic acid synthesis

questions.explanation: Amoxicillin inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis while clavulanate inhibits bacterial beta-lactamase, preventing enzymatic degradation of amoxicillin.

questions.question: By which mechanism does doxycycline exert its bacteriostatic action against susceptible microorganisms?

options.text: Inhibiting bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan cross-linking
Binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis
Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to block peptide chain transpeptidation
Reversibly inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase to halt chromosomal replication

questions.explanation: Doxycycline inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, exerting bacteriostatic activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

questions.question: To avoid compromised absorption, patients taking doxycycline must avoid taking which substances within 2 hours before or after administration?

options.text: Oral contraceptives and low-dose aspirin
ACE inhibitors and statins
Loop diuretics and insulin preparations
Iron supplements, multivitamins, calcium supplements, and antacids

questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly advises not to take iron supplements, multivitamins, calcium supplements, or antacids within 2 hours before or after taking doxycycline.

questions.question: Which bacterial enzyme is directly inhibited by the third-generation respiratory fluoroquinolone levofloxacin?

options.text: DNA gyrase
Dihydrofolate reductase
Beta-lactamase
H+/K+ ATPase

questions.explanation: Levofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that inhibits the bacterial enzyme DNA gyrase, interfering with bacterial DNA replication and repair.

questions.question: Concurrent administration of levofloxacin with which medication class increases the risk of tendon rupture, especially in elderly patients?

options.text: Antacids
Oral contraceptives
Corticosteroids
Benzodiazepines

questions.explanation: Corticosteroids administered concurrently with levofloxacin may increase the risk of tendon rupture, particularly in elderly patients.

questions.question: Which specific hypersensitivity is documented in the lesson as a contraindication to the administration of cefotaxime?

options.text: Hypersensitivity to milk proteins
Hypersensitivity to corn or corn products
Hypersensitivity to iodine-based formulations
Hypersensitivity to adhesive bandaging

questions.explanation: The lesson lists known corn hypersensitivity or hypersensitivity to corn products as a contraindication for cefotaxime.

questions.question: How does co-trimoxazole achieve synergistic antibacterial activity against susceptible bacteria?

options.text: It disrupts outer bacterial membranes and hydrolyzes peptidoglycan cross-links
It simultaneously binds to 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits to block translation
It inhibits both bacterial topoisomerase II and topoisomerase IV enzymes
Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking two consecutive steps in nucleic acid and protein biosynthesis with sulfamethoxazole

questions.explanation: Trimethoprim reversibly inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; together with sulfamethoxazole, co-trimoxazole blocks two consecutive steps in the biosynthesis of nucleic acids and proteins.

questions.question: Which serious gastrointestinal adverse effect develops rarely, but more frequently with lincomycin than with other antibiotics?

options.text: Pseudomembranous colitis
Duodenal ulcer perforation
Esophageal ulceration
Paralytic ileus

questions.explanation: Under lincomycin side-effects, the lesson states that pseudomembranous colitis develops rarely, but more often than with other antibiotics.

subtopics.name: Antiviral Therapeutics
subtopics.description: Mechanisms, clinical indications, and interactions of antiviral agents including acyclovir and oseltamivir.

questions.question: What active intracellular metabolite does acyclovir convert into in order to become part of the viral DNA chain and interfere with viral replication?

options.text: Acyclovir monophosphate
Acyclovir diphosphate
Acyclovir triphosphate
Acyclovir pyrophosphate

questions.explanation: Acyclovir is a synthetic nucleoside that converts to acyclovir triphosphate, which incorporates into the DNA chain and interferes with viral replication.

questions.question: Which concurrent drug may increase the elimination half-life of acyclovir?

options.text: Aminoglycosides
Probenecid
Paracetamol
Cimetidine

questions.explanation: The lesson lists Probenecid under acyclovir interactions as an agent that may increase acyclovir half-life.

questions.question: Which viral enzyme is selectively inhibited by oseltamivir to prevent the replication of influenza A and B viruses?

options.text: Neuraminidase
DNA polymerase
Reverse transcriptase
Thymidine kinase

questions.explanation: Oseltamivir is a selective inhibitor of influenza virus neuraminidase, an enzyme essential for viral replication in influenza A and B.

questions.question: Why should oseltamivir not be administered at the same time as the intranasal influenza vaccine?

options.text: The combination induces severe conjunctivitis and epistaxis
The vaccine drastically decreases oral absorption of oseltamivir
Oseltamivir causes systemic hypersensitivity to the vaccine carrier protein
Oseltamivir may interfere with the immune response to the live intranasal vaccine

questions.explanation: The lesson notes that intranasal influenza vaccine should not be given at the same time because oseltamivir may interfere with the response to the vaccine.

subtopics.name: Antifungal and Anthelmintic Drugs
subtopics.description: Mechanisms, targets, and clinical utility of fluconazole and mebendazole.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of action of fluconazole against susceptible fungi?

options.text: Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to arrest protein translation
Interfering with cytochrome P-450, an enzyme necessary for ergosterol formation
Directly degrading cytoplasmic microtubules and blocking glucose uptake
Inhibiting squalene epoxidase to disrupt fungal wall synthesis

questions.explanation: Fluconazole interferes with cytochrome P-450, an enzyme necessary for fungal ergosterol formation, thereby directly damaging the fungal membrane.

questions.question: By which cellular mechanism does mebendazole eliminate intestinal helminths and their larvae?

options.text: Hyperpolarizing parasite nerve membranes by opening glutamate-gated chloride channels
Inhibiting parasite dihydrofolate reductase to arrest nucleic acid production
Degrading parasite cytoplasmic microtubules and irreversibly blocking glucose uptake
Paralyzing worm musculature through non-competitive nicotinic receptor blockade

questions.explanation: Mebendazole is a synthetic benzimidazole derivative that degrades parasite cytoplasmic microtubules and irreversibly blocks glucose uptake in helminths and larvae.

topics.name: Cardiovascular and Hematologic Pharmacology
topics.description: Therapeutics for hypertension, ischemic heart disease, cardiac arrhythmias, dyslipidemia, and thromboembolic disorders.

subtopics.name: Antihypertensive and Antianginal Drugs
subtopics.description: Calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, beta-blockers, and organic nitrates.

questions.question: How does amlodipine lower systemic blood pressure and relieve angina symptoms?

options.text: Inhibiting calcium movement across cardiac and vascular smooth-muscle membranes, causing vasodilation
Selectively blocking beta-1 adrenergic receptors to decrease myocardial contractile force
Directly inhibiting angiotensin-converting enzyme to reduce angiotensin II formation
Inhibiting sodium-chloride symporters in the distal convoluted tubule

questions.explanation: Amlodipine inhibits calcium movement across cardiac and vascular smooth-muscle cell membranes, dilating coronary and peripheral arteries to decrease peripheral resistance and blood pressure.

questions.question: What is the primary hemodynamic mechanism through which enalapril lowers blood pressure?

options.text: Stimulating cardiac beta-2 receptors to promote coronary artery dilation
Blocking postsynaptic alpha-1 adrenergic receptors in peripheral arterioles
Directly antagonizing L-type calcium channels on vascular smooth muscle
Inhibiting ACE to decrease angiotensin II levels, leading to less vasoconstriction

questions.explanation: Inhibition of ACE by enalapril decreases circulating levels of angiotensin II, leading to less vasoconstriction and lower blood pressure.

questions.question: Losartan reduces peripheral vascular tone and aldosterone secretion by selectively blocking which receptor?

options.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor
Muscarinic M2 receptor
Angiotensin II (AT1) receptor
Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor

questions.explanation: Losartan blocks the angiotensin II (AT1) receptor on specific tissue targets, decreasing vascular tone and aldosterone release.

questions.question: Which receptor-blocking properties characterize the antihypertensive action of carvedilol?

options.text: Selective beta-1 adrenergic blockade without vascular effects
Nonselective beta-blocking and alpha-adrenergic blocking activity
Selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonism and central sympatholysis
Selective muscarinic receptor blockade and potassium channel opening

questions.explanation: Carvedilol possesses nonselective beta-blocking and alpha-adrenergic blocking activity, causing vasodilation and reduced peripheral vascular resistance.

questions.question: How does sublingually administered nitroglycerin acutely relieve angina pectoris?

options.text: Decreases myocardial oxygen demand, reduces left ventricle preload and afterload, and dilates coronary arteries
Decreases heart rate by inhibiting calcium influx into pacemaker cells of the SA node
Constricts systemic veins to shunt pooled venous blood into the pulmonary circulation
Blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors to suppress exercise-induced tachyarrhythmias

questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin decreases myocardial oxygen demand, reduces LV preload and afterload, dilates coronary arteries, and improves collateral blood flow to ischemic myocardium.

questions.question: Concurrent administration of nitroglycerin with phosphodiesterase inhibitors like sildenafil or tadalafil is contraindicated because it produces:

options.text: Severe hypertensive encephalopathy
Acute paradoxical coronary artery spasm
Profound hypotension
Sudden atrioventricular conduction dissociation

questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that concurrent use of nitroglycerin with sildenafil, tadalafil, or avanafil produces hypotension.

questions.question: What is the primary cellular mechanism of action of verapamil in the management of supraventricular tachycardia and angina?

options.text: Selective stimulation of cardiac muscarinic acetylcholine receptors
Direct inhibition of cardiac sodium-potassium ATPase pumps
Antagonism of presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors
Blockade of voltage-gated L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells and cardiomyocytes

questions.explanation: Verapamil blocks voltage-gated L-type Ca++ channels in vascular smooth muscle cells and cardiomyocytes, inhibiting calcium entry into cardiac and vascular cells.

subtopics.name: Anticoagulants, Statins, and Diuretics
subtopics.description: Heparins, HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, and thiazide diuretics.

questions.question: What is the anticoagulant mechanism of dalteparin sodium?

options.text: Directly inhibits thrombin without requiring a plasma cofactor
Potentiates the activity of antithrombin III (ATIII), inhibiting factor Xa and thrombin formation
Inhibits hepatic vitamin K epoxide reductase to block prothrombin synthesis
Irreversibly blocks platelet ADP receptors to inhibit aggregation

questions.explanation: Dalteparin potentiates the activity of ATIII, which inhibits the formation of both factor Xa and thrombin.

questions.question: Dalteparin sodium is strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of which condition?

options.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) or HIT with thrombosis (HITT)
Megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Primary hyperaldosteronism

questions.explanation: Dalteparin is contraindicated in patients with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis (HITT).

questions.question: Which early enzymatic step in cholesterol biosynthesis is inhibited by atorvastatin?

options.text: Squalene monooxygenase
Lipoprotein lipase
HMG-CoA reductase
Thyroxine peroxidase

questions.explanation: Atorvastatin is an antihyperlipidemic agent that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme catalyzing the early rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis.

questions.question: Co-administration of atorvastatin with nicotinic acid increases the risk of which serious musculoskeletal adverse reaction?

options.text: Osteoporosis
Tendon rupture
Osteomalacia
Myopathy or rhabdomyolysis

questions.explanation: The lesson specifically highlights that nicotinic acid increases the risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis when combined with atorvastatin.

questions.question: In which anatomical segment of the renal tubule does hydrochlorothiazide inhibit sodium chloride transport?

options.text: Proximal convoluted tubule
Distal convoluted tubule
Thick ascending limb of Henle
Medullary collecting duct

questions.explanation: Hydrochlorothiazide inhibits sodium chloride transport in the distal convoluted tubule, increasing urinary sodium and fluid excretion.

topics.name: Respiratory and Autonomic Pharmacology
topics.description: Agents modulating bronchial airflow, respiratory secretions, cough reflex, and autonomic cholinergic/adrenergic receptors.

subtopics.name: Bronchodilators and Mucolytics
subtopics.description: Mechanisms and indications of ambroxol, fenoterol, theophylline, and prenoxdiazine.

questions.question: How does the mucolytic agent ambroxol alter sputum characteristics to facilitate airway clearance?

options.text: It disrupts disulfide bonds in the sputum to make it more liquid and increases sputum volume
It disrupts disulfide bonds in the sputum to make it more liquid and increases sputum volume
It dries bronchial secretions through competitive muscarinic receptor blockade
It enhances leukocyte migration to digest mucus plugs enzymatically

questions.explanation: Ambroxol increases sputum volume and makes it less viscid by disrupting disulfide bonds, rendering the sputum more liquid.

questions.question: What intracellular biochemical cascade is activated by fenoterol during an acute bronchospasm?

options.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase leading to intracellular cyclic GMP accumulation
Blockade of muscarinic M3 receptors resulting in protein kinase C inactivation
Stimulation of beta-2 adrenergic receptors activating adenylate cyclase to convert ATP to cyclic AMP
Direct opening of ligand-gated chloride channels in bronchial smooth muscle

questions.explanation: Fenoterol stimulates beta-2 receptors in the lungs, activating adenylate cyclase to convert ATP to cAMP, which causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilation.

questions.question: By what mechanism does prenoxdiazine eliminate unproductive cough?

options.text: Depression of the central cough center in the medulla oblongata
Antagonism of histamine H1 receptors in the upper airway mucosa
Inhibition of pulmonary leukotriene release from sensitized mast cells
Peripheral local anesthesia of the respiratory tract mucosa, suppressing the cough reflex

questions.explanation: Prenoxdiazine is a peripherally acting antitussive that causes anesthesia of the respiratory tract mucosa, suppressing the cough reflex.

questions.question: According to the lesson, which cellular mechanisms contribute to the bronchodilator actions of theophylline?

options.text: Alpha-1 adrenergic agonism and carbonic anhydrase activation
Inhibition of phosphodiesterase, blockade of adenosine receptors, and inhibition of mast cell mediator output
Direct stimulation of muscarinic M2 receptors and activation of vagal efferents
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels and activation of cyclooxygenase

questions.explanation: Theophylline acts by inhibiting phosphodiesterase (raising cAMP), blocking adenosine receptors (stimulating catecholamine release), and inhibiting mediator release from mast cells.

questions.question: What is the therapeutic mechanism of action of atropine in the management of iritis and iridocyclitis?

options.text: Relief of pain by blocking iris sphincter and ciliary muscle contractions, and dilation of the pupil to prevent adhesion formation
Constriction of the pupil to pull the iris away from the trabecular meshwork
Selective alpha-1 adrenergic vasoconstriction of iris microvessels
Topical local anesthesia of corneal sensory nerve fibers

questions.explanation: Atropine relieves iritis pain by blocking contractions of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscles; pupillary dilation also prevents adhesions between the iris and lens.

questions.question: Which ocular adverse effect of atropine accounts for its strict contraindication in patients with glaucoma?

options.text: Corneal neovascularization
Lacrimal duct blockage
Increase of ocular pressure
Retinal pigment epithelium degeneration

questions.explanation: Atropine causes an increase in intraocular pressure, making it contraindicated in glaucoma.

questions.question: How does naphazoline relieve ocular redness, and what is its maximum recommended duration of use?

options.text: Muscarinic blockade of ciliary vessels; use for up to 14 days
Membrane-stabilizing action on mast cells; use continuously for 1 month
Local anesthetic action on conjunctival nerves; single dose only
Sympathomimetic vasoconstriction via alpha adrenergic receptors in conjunctival arterioles; use no longer than 5 days

questions.explanation: Naphazoline is a sympathomimetic that stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors in conjunctival arterioles causing vasoconstriction; the prescription specifies use no longer than 5 days.

topics.name: Neuropsychiatric and Analgesic Pharmacology
topics.description: Centrally acting agents including sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants, nootropics, NSAIDs, and opioid analgesics.

subtopics.name: Central Nervous System Therapeutics
subtopics.description: Benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants, and metabolic nootropic agents.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of diazepam in relieving anxiety, muscle spasms, and seizures?

options.text: Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase in the central synaptic cleft
Inhibition of excitatory synaptic transmission in CNS neurons due to blockade of neurotransmitter release or changes in nerve impulse frequency/amplitude
Post-synaptic blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
Direct inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in cortical and hippocampal synapses

questions.explanation: The lesson describes diazepam's MOA as inhibition of excitatory synaptic transmission in CNS neurons due to blockade of neurotransmitter release or changes of frequency and/or amplitude of nerve impulses.

questions.question: Why are severe hepatic deficiencies (such as hepatitis and liver cirrhosis) listed as contraindications for diazepam?

options.text: Hepatic failure converts diazepam into a potent hepatotoxic metabolite
Hepatic disease induces severe narrow-angle glaucoma upon diazepam exposure
Hepatitis and liver cirrhosis decrease diazepam elimination by a factor of two
Diazepam directly blocks the synthesis of essential clotting factors in the liver

questions.explanation: Under contraindications, the lesson explicitly notes that hepatitis and liver cirrhosis decrease elimination of diazepam by a factor of two.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism of action of the antidepressant maprotiline?

options.text: Tetracyclic antagonist at presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, increasing norepinephrine and serotonin neurotransmission
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor with potent anticholinergic activity
Non-competitive inhibitor of central monoamine oxidase enzymes A and B
Selective dopamine D2 receptor agonist in the mesocortical tract

questions.explanation: Maprotiline is a tetracyclic compound that acts as an antagonist at presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, increasing both norepinephrine and serotonin neurotransmission, with low anticholinergic activity.

questions.question: Which metabolic enhancements and neurotransmitter effects are produced in the brain by piracetam?

options.text: Suppression of cortical glycolysis and blockade of acetylcholine release
Inhibition of neuronal ATP synthesis and blockade of postsynaptic GABA receptors
Opening of neuronal sodium channels to hyperpolarize cortical pyramidal neurons
Activation of glycolysis, increased synthesis of ATP, and increased action of acetylcholine in the CNS

questions.explanation: Piracetam improves brain metabolic processes by activating glycolysis, increasing ATP synthesis, and increasing the action of acetylcholine in the CNS.

questions.question: According to the lesson notes regarding typical first-generation antipsychotics, how is their therapeutic antipsychotic effect produced?

options.text: Agonism of presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors
Post-synaptic blockade at D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway
Selective inhibition of histamine H1 receptors in the basal ganglia
Blockade of NMDA glutamate receptors in the cerebral cortex

questions.explanation: The text states that first-generation antipsychotics produce their antipsychotic effect via post-synaptic blockade at D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway.

subtopics.name: Analgesics and NSAIDs
subtopics.description: Opioid receptor agonists and cyclooxygenase-inhibiting anti-inflammatory analgesics.

questions.question: How is tramadol classified pharmacologically in the management of moderate and neuropathic pain?

options.text: Potent kappa-opioid agonist and calcium channel blocker
Selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor without central opioid activity
Opioid analgesic acting as a weak agonist of mu receptors
Pure opioid receptor antagonist used for reversal of sedation

questions.explanation: Tramadol is classified as an opioid analgesic that functions as a weak agonist of mu receptors.

questions.question: Which serious neurological adverse effect is specifically associated with tramadol administration and withdrawal?

options.text: Increased risk of convulsions due to a decrease in the convulsion threshold
Rapid development of choreiform dyskinesias
Severe ascending Guillain-Barré paralysis
Acute loss of deep tendon reflexes and bilateral mydriasis

questions.explanation: Tramadol lowers the convulsion threshold, increasing the risk of convulsions; its withdrawal symptoms are also accompanied by convulsions.

questions.question: By what mechanism does diclofenac reduce inflammation and alleviate arthritic pain?

options.text: Direct inhibition of leukotriene synthesis from lipoxygenase
Stabilization of mast cell granules and suppression of histamine release
Blockade of substance P receptors on peripheral C-fibers
Inhibition of COX, which is responsible for the synthesis of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid

questions.explanation: Diclofenac's mechanism of action is the inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX), which synthesizes inflammatory prostaglandins from arachidonic acid.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is an absolute contraindication to the administration of ketorolac?

options.text: Allergic conjunctivitis
Active peptic ulcer disease, GI bleeding, or ulceration
Postoperative refractive surgery recovery
Controlled primary hypertension

questions.explanation: Ketorolac is contraindicated in patients with active peptic ulcer disease, chronic GI tract inflammation, and gastrointestinal bleeding or ulceration.

topics.name: Gastrointestinal and Endocrine Pharmacology
topics.description: Therapeutic agents for acid-peptic disorders, GI motility, pancreatic insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, thyroid diseases, and corticosteroid therapy.

subtopics.name: Gastrointestinal Therapeutics
subtopics.description: Proton pump inhibitors, H2 receptor blockers, gastroprotectors, contact laxatives, prokinetics, and digestive enzymes.

questions.question: How does omeprazole inhibit gastric acid secretion for more than 24 hours despite having a short plasma half-life?

options.text: It irreversibly down-regulates parietal cell gastrin receptors
It competitively blocks histamine H2 receptors on parietal basolateral membranes
It accumulates in acidified canaliculi and forms an irreversible disulfide bond with cysteine residues of H+/K+ ATPase
It polymerizes into an insoluble acid-resistant barrier adhering to ulcer craters

questions.explanation: Omeprazole prodrug molecules accumulate in the acidified parietal cell canaliculi and form an irreversible disulfide bond with cysteine residues of the H+/K+ ATPase pump, permanently blocking acid secretion until new pumps are synthesized.

questions.question: What is the primary pharmacological action of the H2 blocker famotidine?

options.text: Decreases gastric acid production, suppresses acid concentration and pepsin content, and reduces secretion volume
Irreversibly inhibits the parietal cell H+/K+ ATP pump, the final step of acid secretion
Chemically neutralizes existing gastric hydrochloric acid upon contact
Stimulates local bicarbonate and mucus synthesis via mucosal prostaglandin agonism

questions.explanation: Famotidine decreases the production of gastric acid, suppresses acid concentration and pepsin content, and decreases the volume of gastric secretion.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the mechanism of action of bismuth subcitrate?

options.text: It exerts strong acid-neutralizing activity and completely suppresses acid secretion
It acts as an irreversible antagonist of parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase
It selectively binds to and blocks gastrin G receptors on ECL cells
It has little acid-neutralizing effect and does not affect acid secretion, but inhibits peptic activity

questions.explanation: Bismuth subcitrate has little acid-neutralizing effect and does not affect acid secretion, but it does inhibit peptic activity.

questions.question: Where and how does the stimulant contact laxative bisacodyl primarily exert its action?

options.text: In the small intestine by delaying osmotic fluid absorption
Mainly on the colon by stimulating enteric neurons to cause peristalsis and increasing fluid and salt secretion
In the stomach by accelerating gastric emptying through vagal stimulation
In the biliary tract by stimulating bile salt secretion into the duodenum

questions.explanation: Bisacodyl stimulates enteric neurons to cause colonic peristalsis and increases fluid/salt secretion; its action on the small intestine is negligible.

questions.question: What dual receptor actions mediate the prokinetic gastrointestinal motility effects of metoclopramide?

options.text: H1 receptor antagonism and D2 receptor agonism
Alpha-1 adrenergic agonism and beta-2 adrenergic blockade
D2 receptor antagonism and 5-HT4 receptor agonism
Muscarinic M1 blockade and 5-HT3 receptor agonism

questions.explanation: Metoclopramide acts via D2 antagonism (blocking dopamine to hasten gastric emptying and enhance LES tone via ACh release) and 5-HT4 agonism (enhancing ACh release from mesenteric motor neurons).

questions.question: Pancreatin is clinically indicated for malabsorption in chronic pancreatitis because it provides a mixture of which enzymes?

options.text: Amylase, lipase, and proteases
Pepsin, renin, and gastrin
Lactase, maltase, and sucrase
Enterokinase, trypsinogen, and carboxypeptidase

questions.explanation: Pancreatin contains mixtures of amylase, lipase, and proteases used to treat malabsorption syndrome due to pancreatic disorders.

subtopics.name: Endocrine and Metabolic Agents
subtopics.description: Antidiabetic drugs, thyroid modulators, anabolic steroids, mineral supplements, and corticosteroids.

questions.question: How does the sulfonylurea glibenclamide stimulate endogenous insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells?

options.text: Stimulating glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptors
Inhibiting dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) enzymes
Opening ATP-sensitive K+ channels to hyperpolarize beta-cell membranes
Inhibition of ATP-sensitive K+ channels, leading to cell depolarization and insulin secretion

questions.explanation: Glibenclamide acts by inhibiting ATP-sensitive K+ channels in pancreatic beta cells, which causes cell depolarization and insulin secretion.

questions.question: What is the primary antihyperglycemic mechanism of action of metformin in type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Direct stimulation of insulin exocytosis from pancreatic islets
Decreasing hepatic production of glucose (inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis) and improving insulin sensitivity
Inhibition of renal sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2)
Enzymatic destruction of complex dietary carbohydrates in the duodenum

questions.explanation: Metformin decreases hepatic production of glucose (inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis), decreases glucose absorption, and improves insulin sensitivity.

questions.question: Besides facilitating glucose uptake into skeletal/cardiac muscle and adipose tissue, insulin facilitates cellular transport of which electrolytes?

options.text: Sodium and chloride
Calcium and phosphate
Potassium and magnesium
Zinc and bicarbonate

questions.explanation: The lesson states that insulin facilitates the passage of glucose, potassium, and magnesium across the cellular membrane of skeletal and cardiac muscle and adipose tissue.

questions.question: What is levothyroxine sodium, and what metabolic effect does it produce in the body?

options.text: Synthetic isomer of thyroxine (T4) that increases basal metabolic rate and is involved in normal growth and development
Antithyroid agent that destroys follicular cells and slows basal metabolism
Rapid-acting T3 preparation used exclusively for emergency thyroid storm
Selective agonist of pituitary TSH receptors that stimulates thyroid hypertrophy

questions.explanation: Levothyroxine sodium is a synthetic isomer of thyroxine (T4) involved in normal metabolism, growth, and development, which increases the basal metabolic rate.

questions.question: By what mechanism does thiamazol treat hyperthyroidism and Graves' disease?

options.text: Destroying hyperfunctioning thyroid follicles via beta emissions
Competitively blocking TSH receptors on thyroid epithelial cells
Accelerating peripheral catabolism and biliary excretion of T3 and T4
Inhibiting thyroxine peroxidase and blocking the synthesis of thyroid hormones

questions.explanation: Thiamazol acts by inhibiting thyroxine peroxidase, thereby blocking the synthesis of thyroid hormones.

questions.question: Which severe adverse hematological condition occurs in 0.1% to 0.5% of patients treated with thiamazol?

options.text: Polycythemia vera
Agranulocytosis
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Essential thrombocythemia

questions.explanation: The lesson notes that thiamazol causes agranulocytosis in 0.1–0.5% of patients.

questions.question: How does the anabolic steroid nandrolone produce its pharmacological effect?

options.text: Stimulates anterior pituitary release of luteinizing hormone and FSH
Blocks peripheral aromatase to prevent conversion of androgens to estrogens
Binds to androgen receptor complex, enters nucleus, and binds directly to specific chromosomal DNA sequences
Directly inhibits renal erythropoietin production to conserve iron stores

questions.explanation: Nandrolone binds to the androgen receptor complex, allowing it to enter the nucleus and bind directly to specific nucleotide sequences of chromosomal DNA to produce androgenic and anabolic effects.

questions.question: How does systemic prednisolone suppress inflammation and tissue responses in severe bronchial asthma?

options.text: Inhibits accumulation of inflammatory cells at sites, phagocytosis, lysosomal enzyme release/synthesis, and inflammatory mediator release
Directly activates airway adenylate cyclase to elevate intracellular cAMP
Competitively antagonizes leukotriene C4 receptors on airway smooth muscle
Selectively inhibits cyclooxygenase-2 without suppressing cell-mediated immunity

questions.explanation: Prednisolone inhibits accumulation of inflammatory cells at inflammation sites, phagocytosis, lysosomal enzyme release/synthesis, and release of inflammatory mediators, while suppressing cell-mediated immune reactions.

questions.question: Which specific condition is listed in the lesson as a contraindication to the administration of fluticasone?

options.text: Seasonal allergic rhinitis
Steroid responsive dermatological pruritus
Mild chronic stable angina
Severe allergy to milk proteins

questions.explanation: Fluticasone lists severe allergy to milk proteins, untreated localized infection of nasal mucosa, and formulation hypersensitivity as contraindications.

questions.question: What is the biological mechanism of action of ferrous sulfate when administered for anemia?

options.text: Stimulates renal secretion of erythropoietin via tissue hypoxia pathways
Acts as a biological cofactor for dihydrofolate reductase in thymidylate synthesis
Combines with porphyrin and globin chains to form hemoglobin, critical for tissue oxygen delivery
Promotes intrinsic factor secretion in the stomach to boost cyanocobalamin absorption

questions.explanation: Iron from ferrous sulfate combines with porphyrin and globin chains to form hemoglobin, which is critical for oxygen delivery from the lungs to other tissues.
